title: Differential equations, order, solutions, integral curves, and IVPs
section: Introduction ▷ Differential equations and initial conditions
terms: differential equation; ordinary differential equation; partial differential equation; order; solution; general solution; particular solution; integral curve; initial condition; initial value problem.

exposition.text:
A differential equation relates an unknown function to its derivatives. An ordinary differential
equation (ODE) uses one independent variable; a partial differential equation (PDE) uses par-
tial derivatives in several variables. Its order is the highest derivative present, even when that
derivative occurs nonlinearly. An apparently nonlinear equation may simplify algebraically, so
factor or complete a square in its derivative before choosing a solution method. A solution is a
sufficiently differentiable function satisfying the equation throughout an interval or region.
A general solution describes a family; a particular solution selects a member. An initial value
problem (IVP) adds values of the function and, for higher order equations, derivatives at one
point. Integral curves are solution graphs, sometimes described implicitly by F (x, y) = C.

Existence or uniqueness is not automatic: standard first-order uniqueness holds locally when
the right side is continuous and locally Lipschitz in the dependent variable.

question.text:
3 2 2 4 4
For an unknown function u(x, y), the equation (∂ u/∂x ∂y) + ∂ u/∂y = 0 is which type?
(A) A second-order nonlinear ODE
(B) A third-order linear PDE
(C) A fourth-order nonlinear PDE
(D) A sixth-order nonlinear PDE
(E) A fourth-order linear ODE

solution.text:
The unknown depends on two independent variables and partial derivatives appear, so it is
a PDE. The highest differentiation order is four. Squaring a third derivative does not turn
it into a sixth derivative, but it does make the equation nonlinear.

question.text:
′ 2/3
How many continuously differentiable solutions on R satisfy y = 3|y| and y(0) = 0?
(A) None (B) Exactly one (C) Exactly two (D) Exactly three (E) Infinitely many

solution.text:
3
For every a ≥ 0, define y(x) = 0 for x ≤ a and y(x) = (x − a) for x ≥ a. The values and
first derivatives match at a, and direct substitution verifies the equation everywhere. All
satisfy the initial condition and are distinct. The right side is continuous but not locally
Lipschitz in y at zero, so standard uniqueness does not apply.
